Course overview

ID 553: Introduction to the Principles of Instructional Design

A fully online, eight-module graduate-level introduction to instructional design. You will study the major ID models, analyze two realistic design cases, conduct learner and task analyses, write aligned objectives and assessments, plan and prototype an instructional intervention, and design its evaluation. The course follows the ADDIE arc (analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation) while treating it critically, and every module produces a component of a final instructional plan you can carry into practice.

Audience: Graduate students and practitioners new to instructional design: teachers, trainers, faculty developers, and technologists.
Duration: Eight modules over 8 to 15 weeks. Plan on 6 to 8 hours per module.
Instructor: Idowu David Awoyemi, The University of Alabama

Introduction Module

Course orientation, expectations, and your first discussion.

Page

Welcome to ID 553

Welcome to ID 553. This course introduces the principles and practice of instructional design (ID): the systematic process of analyzing learning needs, designing and developing instruction, and evaluating whether it worked. You will leave with a working knowledge of the major ID models, experience analyzing realistic design cases, and a complete instructional plan of your own.

Course description

An intensive introduction to the principles associated with designing instruction for classroom, workplace, and online settings. Topics include the history and models of instructional design, front-end analysis (learner, context, and task), learning objectives and aligned assessment, instructional strategies, multimedia and accessibility principles, rapid prototyping, and formative and summative evaluation. Two case analyses develop professional judgment; a staged instructional plan develops practical skill. Three credit hours.

Who this course is for

  • Teachers who want to design instruction more deliberately.
  • Trainers and faculty developers who build courses and workshops.
  • Technologists and media specialists who work with subject-matter experts.
  • Graduate students preparing for advanced ID coursework or research.

No prior ID coursework is assumed.

Course objectives

By the end of this course you will be able to:

  1. Describe the origins, purposes, and major models of instructional design and select a model appropriate to a given context.
  2. Analyze an instructional design case, identify the underlying design problem, and recommend a defensible course of action.
  3. Conduct learner, context, and task analyses for a real instructional need.
  4. Write measurable learning objectives and design assessments aligned with them.
  5. Plan an instructional intervention that applies evidence-based strategies and multimedia and accessibility principles.
  6. Design a formative and summative evaluation for the intervention.
  7. Reflect critically on your own design decisions and on the limits of the models you use.

How to Succeed in This Course

This page tells you how the course runs week to week and what the instructor expects. Read it once now and again before your first case analysis.

The weekly rhythm

Each module follows the same pattern. Plan about six to eight hours per module.

  1. Read the module pages and any linked readings. Take notes in your own words; you will reuse them in the assignments.
  2. Check your understanding with the knowledge check. It is short, low-stakes, and can be retaken.
  3. Discuss. Post in the module discussion by midweek and reply to peers by the end of the module. Discussions are where the field's judgment calls get argued out; treat them as seminar, not as a box to tick.
  4. Produce. Complete the module assignment. Every assignment builds toward the final instructional plan, so keep your files organized in one folder.

The design project runs through the course

Choose an instructional problem in Module 1 and keep it for the whole course. Good problems are real, bounded, and involve learners you can actually talk to: a unit in your classroom, an onboarding topic at your workplace, a skill your colleagues keep asking about. Assignments 5, 6, and 7 all apply to this one problem. Choosing something too large ("a course on leadership") makes every later assignment harder. Choosing something concrete ("teaching new tutors to run a 30-minute writing conference") makes them easier and more useful.

Writing expectations

  • Follow APA 7th edition for citations and references.
  • Write in clear, direct prose. Headings help. Bullet lists are fine for analyses; use paragraphs for arguments.
  • Cite the module readings when you use their ideas, and cite outside sources when you use those. A claim about what "research shows" needs a source.

Using generative AI in this course

You may use generative AI tools to brainstorm, outline, check clarity, and summarize readings for your own study. You may not submit AI-generated text as your analysis, reflection, or design rationale. Those are the evidence of your thinking and are the basis of your grade.

When you use AI in any assignment, add a one-line disclosure at the end: the tool, what you used it for, and what you did yourself. Undisclosed AI-generated submissions are treated as academic misconduct under university policy.

You are also welcome, and encouraged, to treat AI tools as a design topic: several assignments let you propose AI-supported instruction, and the second case is about AI literacy.

Late work and extensions

Assignments are due at 11:59 p.m. Central time on the date in the course schedule. One 48-hour extension per student is available on request, no reason needed, if requested before the deadline. Beyond that, late work loses 10% per day up to five days.

Accessibility

If you need accommodations, contact the Office of Disability Services and let the instructor know as early as possible. Course pages are built to WCAG 2.2 AA; if you encounter something that does not work with your assistive technology, report it and it will be fixed.

Getting help

  • Course logistics: post in the "Questions" thread of the Introduction Discussion.
  • Content questions: the module discussion.
  • Private matters: email the instructor.
  • Technical problems with the LMS: your institution's help desk.

Module 1: Introduction to Instructional Design Models

What instructional design is, where it came from, and the models that organize the work.

Page

What Is Instructional Design?

Estimated reading time: 25 minutes.

A working definition

Instructional design is the systematic process of translating principles of learning and instruction into plans for instructional materials, activities, resources, and evaluation. Three words in that definition carry most of the weight:

  • Systematic. ID proceeds through identifiable phases with outputs that feed the next phase. It is not a recipe, but it is not improvisation either.
  • Principles of learning. ID rests on evidence about how people learn: cognitive load, retrieval practice, feedback, transfer, motivation. A designer who ignores that evidence is decorating, not designing.
  • Plans. The product of ID is a plan that someone can implement, evaluate, and revise. The plan may be a lesson, a course, a job aid, a simulation, or a curriculum.

Instructional design is also a profession with its own standards. The International Board of Standards for Training, Performance and Instruction (IBSTPI) publishes competencies for instructional designers organized around professional foundations, planning and analysis, design and development, evaluation and implementation, and management. Keep those five areas in mind; this course visits each.

Where instructional design came from

The field has three roots that still shape it.

Military and industrial training (1940s onward). During the Second World War, psychologists including Robert Gagné were asked to train large numbers of people quickly and reliably on complex equipment. They developed task analysis, criterion-referenced testing, and the practice of specifying objectives before building instruction. The systems approach that emerged, in which instruction is a set of interacting components engineered toward a measurable outcome, is the ancestor of every ID model you will study.

Behavioral and cognitive psychology (1950s to 1980s). Skinner's programmed instruction contributed small steps, active responding, and immediate feedback. Mager's Preparing Instructional Objectives (1962) gave designers a format for writing measurable objectives. Gagné's Conditions of Learning (1965) argued that different types of learning outcomes require different instructional conditions, and his nine events of instruction became the most widely used lesson framework in the field. Cognitive psychology later reframed learning as the construction of mental models and drew attention to working memory limits, prior knowledge, and transfer.

Constructivism and learning sciences (1990s onward). Constructivist critiques argued that the systems approach could produce sterile, decontextualized instruction. Situated learning, problem-based learning, cognitive apprenticeship, and learner-centered design pushed the field toward authentic tasks, collaboration, and reflection. The learning sciences added design-based research and a closer partnership with cognitive science. Contemporary ID draws on all three roots and argues about their balance.

The systems view

The most durable idea in ID is that instruction is a system: a set of components (learners, content, methods, media, environment, assessment) whose interactions determine the outcome. Change one component and the others shift. Add a video and you change the cognitive load; move a course online and you change the social presence; shorten the practice and you change retention.

Two consequences follow. First, analysis comes before design because you cannot engineer a system you have not described. Second, evaluation is part of the system, not an afterthought; every ID model closes the loop with data.

What instructional designers actually do

A typical project involves:

  1. Needs assessment. Is there a performance gap, and is instruction the right solution? Often it is not; a job aid, a process change, or a better incentive may fix the problem faster. Designers who skip this question build training nobody needed.
  2. Front-end analysis. Who are the learners, what is the context, and what exactly must learners be able to do (Module 3)?
  3. Design. Objectives, assessments, sequence, strategies, and media selection (Modules 4 and 6).
  4. Development. Producing materials, often with subject-matter experts, media producers, and developers (Module 6).
  5. Implementation. Delivering the instruction and supporting facilitators and learners.
  6. Evaluation. Formative evaluation while building, summative evaluation after delivery, and revision (Module 7).
  7. Project management. Scope, schedule, stakeholders, and budget. Rarely taught, always present.

Instructional design and teaching

Teachers design instruction every day. What distinguishes ID as a discipline is the explicitness and the systems view: objectives are written, assessments are aligned before activities are chosen, and the design is documented so others can implement and evaluate it. Many teachers find that learning ID makes their tacit expertise visible, and that visibility is what makes it improvable.

Key terms

Instructional designSystematic process of planning instruction from analysis through evaluation

Needs assessmentDetermining whether a performance gap exists and whether instruction can close it
Front-end analysisLearner, context, and task analysis conducted before design
Criterion-referenced assessmentMeasuring performance against a standard rather than against other learners

A Survey of Instructional Design Models

Estimated reading time: 35 minutes. Read the ADDIE overview and Merrill's First Principles (linked in this module) before this page.

Why models?

An instructional design model is a representation of the design process: what to do, in what order, and what each step produces. Models serve three purposes. They communicate the process to clients and teammates. They structure the work so nothing essential is skipped. And they embed assumptions about learning and about how design should proceed, which is why choosing a model is a design decision in its own right.

No model is the field's official one. Practitioners adapt, combine, and abandon models as projects demand. Your job in this course is to know the major models well enough to choose and adapt deliberately.

ADDIE

ADDIE is less a specific model than a family name for the generic systems approach: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation. The label was applied retroactively in the 1990s to processes that had existed since the 1970s.

PhaseCore questionsTypical outputs
AnalysisIs there a gap? Who are the learners? What must they do? What constraints apply?Needs assessment, learner and context analysis, task analysis
DesignWhat objectives, assessments, sequence, strategies, and media?Design document, objectives, assessment plan, storyboards
DevelopmentBuild itMaterials, media, prototypes, facilitator guides
ImplementationDeliver it and support itDelivery plan, training for facilitators, learner support
EvaluationDid it work? How do we improve it?Formative and summative evaluation reports, revision plan

Strengths: universally understood, complete, adaptable. Weaknesses: often practiced as a rigid waterfall with evaluation stuck at the end, slow when requirements change, and easy to bloat with documentation. Most later models are responses to those weaknesses.

Dick and Carey Systems Approach Model

Walter Dick and Lou Carey's model (first published 1978, now in its eighth edition with James Carey) is the most detailed articulation of the systems view. It has ten interconnected components:

  1. Identify instructional goals
  2. Conduct instructional analysis
  3. Analyze learners and contexts
  4. Write performance objectives
  5. Develop assessment instruments
  6. Develop instructional strategy
  7. Develop and select instructional materials
  8. Design and conduct formative evaluation
  9. Revise instruction
  10. Design and conduct summative evaluation

Two features matter most. First, objectives are written before assessments, and assessments before strategies, which guarantees alignment. Second, revision is a loop, fed by formative evaluation, that touches every earlier component. Dick and Carey is the model behind Modules 3, 4, 6, and 7 of this course.

Morrison, Ross, Kemp

The Kemp model (Morrison, Ross, Kalman, and Kemp) presents nine elements in a circle rather than a line: instructional problems, learner characteristics, task analysis, instructional objectives, content sequencing, instructional strategies, designing the message, instructional delivery, and evaluation instruments. The circular layout signals that a designer can start anywhere and that the elements are interdependent. Surrounding the circle are ongoing processes: planning, project management, support services, and formative and summative evaluation. Kemp is well suited to classroom teachers and to projects where constraints, not objectives, drive the design.

Successive Approximation Model (SAM)

Michael Allen's SAM (2012) is an agile alternative to ADDIE. After a brief preparation phase (information gathering and a "savvy start" kickoff), the project cycles through iterative design (prototype, review, design) and iterative development (develop, implement, evaluate) with stakeholders reviewing working prototypes early and often. The core commitment is that a rough prototype reviewed in week two teaches the team more than a design document approved in week six. SAM fits e-learning projects with uncertain requirements and available stakeholders; it fits poorly where sign-off must precede any building.

Backward Design (Understanding by Design)

Wiggins and McTighe's Understanding by Design (1998, 2005) is a curriculum design framework rather than a full process model, but its three stages reorganize how designers think:

  1. Identify desired results (enduring understandings, essential questions, objectives).
  2. Determine acceptable evidence (assessments, especially performance tasks).
  3. Plan learning experiences and instruction.

The insight is the order: evidence before activities. Teachers frequently plan activities first and assessments last, which produces engaging lessons that do not teach what was intended. Backward Design shares this commitment with Dick and Carey but expresses it in language closer to classroom practice.

Merrill's First Principles of Instruction

David Merrill (2002) reviewed the major instructional theories and models and extracted five principles they share. Learning is promoted when:

  1. Learners are engaged in solving real-world problems (problem-centered).
  2. Existing knowledge is activated as a foundation for new knowledge.
  3. New knowledge is demonstrated to the learner.
  4. New knowledge is applied by the learner.
  5. New knowledge is integrated into the learner's world.

First Principles is not a process model; it is a set of criteria any instruction should meet. Use it as a checklist against your designs. Instruction that only demonstrates (a lecture) or only applies (an unguided project) fails the principles.

Rapid prototyping and design thinking

Beyond named models, two broader movements shape current practice. Rapid prototyping (Tripp and Bichelmeyer, 1990) argues that in ill-structured domains, building a quick working version and testing it with learners is a better form of analysis than more analysis. Design thinking, imported from product design, emphasizes empathy with users, reframing the problem, ideation, prototyping, and testing. Both push against the linear reading of ADDIE and both appear in Module 6.

Comparing the models

ModelProcess shapeEmphasisBest fit
ADDIELinear with feedbackCompletenessLarge, well-defined projects; shared vocabulary
Dick and CareyLinear with revision loopAlignment and formative evaluationSystematic training design; instruction with clear performance outcomes
KempCircularFlexibility; constraintsClassroom and small-team design
SAMIterative cyclesPrototypes; stakeholder reviewE-learning with uncertain requirements
Backward DesignThree stagesEvidence before activitiesCurriculum and unit planning
First PrinciplesCriteria, not processProblem-centered instructionQuality check on any design

Choosing a model

Ask four questions:

  1. How well defined is the problem? Well defined favors Dick and Carey or ADDIE; ill defined favors SAM or rapid prototyping.
  2. How available are stakeholders and learners? Iterative models need them often.
  3. What does the client expect? Some organizations require design documents before development; others want to see something working.
  4. What is the risk of getting it wrong? High-stakes performance (medical, safety) favors the rigor of Dick and Carey; low-stakes exploration tolerates iteration.

In practice, most designers use an ADDIE skeleton with iterative development inside it and Merrill's principles as a quality check. That hybrid is a legitimate answer in this course, as long as you can justify it.

Quiz

Module 1 Knowledge Check

Eight questions on the foundations and models of instructional design. Unlimited attempts; best score counts.

1.

Which statement best captures the systems view of instruction?

Answer: Instruction is a set of interacting components whose interactions determine the outcome, so changing one component affects the others
The systems view is why analysis precedes design and evaluation closes the loop.
2.

A manager asks you to build a course because sales are down. Which instructional design step should come first?

Answer: Conduct a needs assessment to determine whether a performance gap exists and whether instruction can close it
Many performance problems are not training problems. Needs assessment decides whether instruction is the right solution.
3.

In the Dick and Carey model, which order guarantees alignment?

Answer: Objectives, then assessments, then strategies
Objectives first, assessments second, strategies third. The same logic underlies Backward Design.
4.

Which model cycles through prototype, review, and revision with stakeholders reviewing working versions early and often?

Answer: Successive Approximation Model (SAM)
SAM is the agile alternative to a linear ADDIE.
5.

Which of the following are among Merrill's First Principles of Instruction? Select all that apply.

Answer: Learners engage in solving real-world problems; Existing knowledge is activated; New knowledge is demonstrated; New knowledge is applied by the learner; New knowledge is integrated into the learner's world
Problem-centered, activation, demonstration, application, integration. Delivery mode is not a principle.
6.

Backward Design asks the designer to plan learning activities before deciding what evidence of learning will be acceptable.

Answer: False
Backward Design plans desired results first, acceptable evidence second, and learning experiences third.
7.

The Kemp model is drawn as a circle rather than a line to signal that:

Answer: The designer can begin with any element and the elements are interdependent
The circular layout expresses flexibility and interdependence, with ongoing processes surrounding the elements.
8.

Which pairing of problem type and model is most defensible?

Answer: High-stakes safety procedure with clear performance outcomes: Dick and Carey
High-stakes, well-defined performance favors the rigor and formative evaluation of Dick and Carey.

Module 2: ID Case Analysis I

Learn the case method and analyze your first instructional design case.

Page

How to Analyze an Instructional Design Case

Estimated reading time: 20 minutes.

Why cases?

Instructional design is a profession of judgment. Models tell you what steps to take; they do not tell you what to do when the client wants a course but needs a job aid, when the subject-matter expert will not return your calls, or when the budget disappears halfway through development. Case analysis develops the judgment that models cannot supply. It is the method used in The ID CaseBook (Ertmer, Quinn, and Glazewski) and in professional preparation across law, medicine, and business.

A case is a realistic, incomplete, and messy account of a design situation. It has more information than you need and less than you want. Your task is not to find the right answer, because there usually is not one, but to construct a defensible analysis: one that identifies the real problem, weighs the constraints and stakeholders, and recommends action that a professional could justify.

The six-step framework

Use these steps for both case analyses in this course. Write a heading for each in your submission.

1. Summarize the situation

In one paragraph, state who is involved, what is being asked, and what has happened so far. Resist the urge to interpret yet. A reader who has not seen the case should understand the setup from your summary.

2. Identify the stakeholders and their interests

List every person or group with a stake in the outcome, and for each, what they want and what they fear. Include the learners, who are often absent from the conversation in the case. Note where interests conflict.

3. Frame the design problem

This is the heart of the analysis. The presenting request ("build us a course") is rarely the problem. Ask:

  • Is there a performance gap, and is it caused by lack of knowledge or skill, or by something else (tools, incentives, process, environment)?
  • What constraints are fixed (deadline, budget, policy) and which are negotiable?
  • What is unknown that matters, and how could it be found out?

State the problem in one or two sentences. A good problem statement names the gap, the learners, and the constraint that makes it hard.

4. Generate and weigh alternatives

Propose at least three courses of action. One should be the obvious one the client asked for; one should be a non-instructional or partly instructional alternative; one should be something a less experienced designer would not think of. For each, list the main benefits, costs, and risks, and identify which stakeholders would favor or resist it.

5. Recommend and justify

Choose one alternative (or a sequence). Justify it with reference to the problem statement, the stakeholders, the constraints, and at least one principle or model from the course. Say what you would do in the first two weeks.

6. Anticipate consequences and plan evaluation

What could go wrong with your recommendation? What early indicators would tell you it is working or not? What would you do if it fails?

Common mistakes

  • Solving the presenting request. The client asked for a course, so you design a course. Check first whether instruction is the right lever.
  • Ignoring the learners. Cases are told from the designer's or client's perspective. Ask what the learners already know, what they need, and how they would experience each alternative.
  • Treating constraints as fixed. Budgets, timelines, and formats are often more negotiable than the case implies, but you have to say how you would negotiate.
  • Recommending without trade-offs. If your recommendation has no downside, you have not looked hard enough.
  • Retelling the case. Summarize briefly; spend your words on analysis.

What a strong analysis looks like

A strong analysis is specific to the case, cites evidence from it (quote or paraphrase what people said and what the data showed), applies course concepts by name, and reads like a memo a designer would actually write for a client. It is usually 1,500 to 2,000 words. It takes a position and defends it while acknowledging what a reasonable colleague might do differently.

Practice

Before you read Case 1, take any situation from your own work where someone asked for training. Run it through steps 2 and 3 in ten minutes. Was the presenting request the real problem? Bring your example to the Case 1 discussion.

Reference

Ertmer, P. A., Quinn, J. A., & Glazewski, K. D. (Eds.). (2019). The ID CaseBook: Case studies in instructional design (5th ed.). Routledge.

Page

Case 1: Onboarding at Crestview Regional Hospital

This case is fictional. Any resemblance to real organizations or people is coincidental.

The request

Maya Okafor had been the sole instructional designer at Crestview Regional Hospital for fourteen months when the Chief Nursing Officer, Dr. Ellen Vance, stopped by her office on a Tuesday afternoon.

"We're going live with the new electronic health record on March 3," Dr. Vance said. "That's eleven weeks. I need every nurse trained before then. Four hundred and twelve nurses across three shifts, plus about sixty per-diem staff. The vendor gave us an eight-hour classroom course. I need you to make it work."

Maya asked what "make it work" meant.

"The vendor course is eight hours in a computer lab with a vendor trainer. We have one lab with sixteen seats. Do the math. And the last time we did a system change, in 2021, we ran classroom training for everyone and the help desk still got nine hundred calls in the first week. The unit managers are already telling me their people don't have time. I need something better than last time, and I need it in eleven weeks."

The organization

Crestview is a 380-bed regional hospital serving a mostly rural area. It employs about 2,100 people. Nursing turnover is 19% a year, slightly above the national average. About a third of the nurses have been at Crestview for more than ten years; about a quarter have been there less than two.

The hospital is replacing a fifteen-year-old electronic health record (EHR) with a modern system from a national vendor. The new system changes how nurses document assessments, administer medications (with barcode scanning at the bedside), and hand off patients between shifts. Physicians, pharmacists, and unit clerks are also affected, but their training is being handled by their own departments.

The nursing education department consists of Maya, a nursing professional development specialist named Carlos Reyes (a registered nurse with twenty years of bedside experience and no formal training background), and an administrative assistant. The hospital uses a learning management system for annual compliance modules; nurses generally regard it as a place where mandatory videos live. Each unit has a computer on wheels for every two or three nurses and a break room with one desktop.

What Maya learned in the first week

Maya spent the first week talking to people. Her notes:

Vendor training team. The eight-hour course covers every nursing function in the system. The vendor also offers a "train the trainer" program (three days, off-site, for up to twelve people) and a practice environment ("the playground") where users can log in and try workflows with fake patients. The vendor trainer said, "Honestly, most hospitals do the eight hours, and then everyone forgets it by go-live because it's six weeks later."

Unit managers. Of the eleven unit managers Maya reached, nine said they could not release nurses for a full day; the most any would commit was two four-hour blocks, and only if backfill was paid. Two managers asked whether training could be "done on the unit during downtime." One said, "My night shift people will not come in on their day off for a class, and I don't blame them."

Nurses. Maya shadowed on two units and talked informally with nineteen nurses. Themes: the old system is hated but familiar; barcode medication scanning is the biggest worry ("What happens when the scanner doesn't read the band?"); several younger nurses had used the new vendor's system at a previous employer or in nursing school; several veteran nurses said they "aren't computer people" and were anxious. Almost everyone said the 2021 training was "a waste of a day" because "you can't remember eight hours of clicking."

Help desk data from 2021. Maya pulled the ticket log from the 2021 change. Of the roughly 900 first-week calls, 61% concerned five workflows: logging in, finding a patient, documenting vitals, medication administration, and shift handoff. Most calls came from the day shift on medical-surgical units in the first three days.

Super users. Carlos suggested a "super user" program: two or three nurses per unit trained more deeply who then support their peers at go-live. In 2021 there had been super users, but they were chosen by managers based on who was available, and several told Carlos they "didn't feel like they knew any more than anyone else."

Budget. Dr. Vance has authorized overtime backfill for training up to $85,000. The vendor's train-the-trainer program costs $18,000 plus travel. There is no budget for additional instructional design staff. The LMS can host SCORM modules and videos and can track completion.

Timeline. The playground environment will be available in three weeks. Go-live is in eleven weeks. Vendor trainers are on site for the two weeks before go-live and the week after.

The complication

On Friday, Dr. Vance forwarded Maya an email from the Chief Financial Officer: "Our regulatory advisor reminds us that documented competency for each nurse on medication administration in the new system is required before they administer meds after go-live. Please confirm the training plan includes a completion record for every nurse." Dr. Vance added one line: "This is now a compliance issue. Whatever you design has to produce a record. Let's meet Monday."

Maya looked at her calendar. She had ten weeks and four days.

Questions to consider

These are prompts for your analysis, not the required structure. Use the six-step framework from the case method page.

  • What is the actual design problem here, and how does it differ from "deliver the vendor's eight-hour course to 470 people"?
  • What do the 2021 help desk data tell you about what the training should prioritize?
  • Which of Maya's constraints are truly fixed? Which are negotiable, and with whom?
  • How should the differences among nurses (experience with the vendor system, comfort with technology, shift) shape the design?
  • What role could the playground environment, super users, and the LMS play, and what are the risks of each?
  • How does the compliance requirement change the design, and how can it be satisfied without turning the whole program into a checkbox?
  • What would you do in the first two weeks?
Discussion forum

Case 1 Discussion: Framing the Problem

Before writing your full analysis, test your framing of the Crestview case against your classmates'.

Initial post (by midweek). In no more than 250 words:

  1. State the design problem in one or two sentences, using the guidance on the case method page (name the gap, the learners, and the constraint that makes it hard).
  2. Name the one piece of evidence in the case that most shaped your framing, and say why.
  3. Identify one thing Maya does not know that you would want to find out before designing, and how you would find it.

Replies (by end of module). Reply to two classmates whose problem statements differ from yours. Say specifically where they differ and which framing you find more defensible, with reference to the case. Changing your own framing after the discussion is expected and is a sign the method is working.

Module 3: Examining the Situation: Learner and Task Analysis

Front-end analysis: who the learners are, where they will learn, and what exactly they must be able to do.

Page

Learner and Context Analysis

Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

Why analyze learners?

Every design decision assumes something about the learners: what they already know, what they can attend to, what motivates them, what tools they have, and how much time they will give you. If those assumptions are wrong, the instruction fails no matter how well built. Learner analysis replaces assumptions with evidence. Context analysis does the same for the settings in which learning and performance happen.

In the Dick and Carey model, this is component 3, "Analyze learners and contexts." In ADDIE it belongs to Analysis. In Kemp it is "learner characteristics." Every model has it because skipping it is the most common cause of instruction that is accurate, well produced, and useless.

What to find out about learners

Dick and Carey organize learner characteristics into categories. Adapted and consolidated:

CategoryQuestionsWhy it matters
Entry skillsWhat prerequisite knowledge and skills do learners have? Which are missing?Determines where instruction starts; missing prerequisites derail everything after
Prior knowledge of the topicWhat do they already know, including misconceptions?Prior knowledge is the strongest predictor of new learning; misconceptions must be addressed, not overwritten
Attitudes toward content and deliveryDo they see the content as relevant? How do they feel about the delivery mode (online, classroom, self-paced)?Shapes motivation and the need for relevance-building
MotivationWhy are they here? What are the consequences of learning or not learning?Keller's ARCS (attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction) gives design levers
Educational and ability levelsReading level, language, numeracy, digital skillsSets the register of materials and the need for supports
Learning preferencesHow do they prefer to learn, and how do they actually learn best?Preferences inform engagement; do not confuse preferences with "learning styles," which lack empirical support as a basis for matching instruction
Attitudes toward the organizationTrust, morale, history with trainingExplains resistance and predicts uptake
Group characteristicsSize, heterogeneity, existing relationshipsDetermines whether one design fits all, and whether collaboration is feasible

Add for adult learners: competing demands on time, relevant experience that can be leveraged, and the degree of autonomy they expect (Knowles's andragogy).

How to find out

Use more than one method; each has blind spots.

  • Interviews with a sample of learners and with their supervisors or teachers. Ask about the task, not about training: "Walk me through the last time you did this."
  • Observation of learners performing the task or a related one. Watch for workarounds; they reveal what the current process fails to support.
  • Surveys for breadth across a large population. Keep them short; ask about specifics (tools used, years of experience, prior exposure) rather than self-rated confidence alone.
  • Existing data: performance records, help desk logs, assessment results, completion data, error reports. These are often the most objective evidence and the least used.
  • Pre-tests or diagnostic tasks for entry skills when the stakes justify it.

Triangulate. If interviews say learners are confident and error logs say they fail, believe the logs and ask why the confidence exists.

Context analysis

Dick and Carey distinguish two contexts.

Performance context: where learners will use what they learn. Analyze the physical setting (space, noise, equipment), the social setting (alone or with others, supervision), the managerial support (is the new performance expected and rewarded?), and the relevance of the skill to the job. If the performance context does not support the new behavior, training will not produce it.

Learning context: where instruction will happen. Analyze the facilities and equipment (labs, devices, bandwidth, LMS), the compatibility of the site with your instructional needs, the constraints on time and scheduling, and the fit between the learning context and the performance context. The closer the two, the better the transfer; that is why simulation, practice environments, and on-the-job components matter.

From analysis to design decisions

Analysis is only useful if it changes the design. For every finding, write an implication. Examples:

FindingDesign implication
A quarter of nurses have used the vendor system elsewhereOffer a test-out or an accelerated path; do not force experienced users through basics
Night shift will not attend daytime classesProvide asynchronous options and on-unit support during night hours
Help desk calls concentrated in five workflowsPrioritize those workflows for practice; build job aids for them
Veteran nurses report technology anxietyBuild confidence early with a guaranteed-success first task; pair with peer support
Learners have two devices per three people on the unitDesign practice that can be done in short sessions at shared devices; avoid requiring personal devices

Common mistakes

  • Describing learners in demographics only ("adults aged 25 to 60") with no implications.
  • Assuming homogeneity; most populations have subgroups that need different paths.
  • Relying on self-report alone.
  • Analyzing the learning context but not the performance context, and then wondering why nothing transferred.
  • Treating "learning styles" as a basis for design.

Preparing for Assignment 5

Choose at least two methods and gather real data about the learners for your course design project, even if the sample is small (three interviews and a review of existing records is enough). If you cannot reach the learners at all, reconsider the project; a design built on imagined learners will not survive the later assignments.

Page

Task Analysis

Estimated reading time: 35 minutes.

What task analysis is for

Task analysis answers the question: what, exactly, must the learner be able to do, and what does that performance consist of? It turns a goal ("nurses will administer medications safely in the new system") into a map of the knowledge, skills, and decisions the goal requires. That map determines the objectives (Module 4), the sequence and strategies (Module 6), and the assessments. Without it, designers teach what they happen to know rather than what the performance requires.

Dick and Carey call this "instructional analysis" and split it into two questions: what type of learning is the goal, and what subordinate skills does it require?

Step 1: Classify the goal

Gagné's taxonomy of learning outcomes is the standard classification. The type of outcome determines the analysis method and, later, the instructional conditions.

Outcome typeWhat the learner doesExampleAnalysis method
Verbal informationStates, recalls, describesName the five rights of medication administrationCluster analysis: group the information into logical sets
Intellectual skillsDiscriminates, classifies, applies rules, solves problemsDecide whether a scanned wristband matches the orderHierarchical analysis: identify subordinate skills
Cognitive strategiesManages own thinking and learningChoose a checking strategy under time pressureHierarchical analysis plus the intellectual skills it governs
Motor skillsPerforms a physical procedureScan a wristband with a handheld scannerProcedural analysis: list the steps in order
AttitudesChooses to act in a certain wayChoose to scan every time, even when the scanner is slowAnalyze the behavior chosen and the intellectual skills and information that support it

Most real goals combine types. A procedural task includes decisions (intellectual skills) at branch points and requires information at several steps. Classify the overall goal, then classify each component as you decompose it.

Step 2: Decompose the goal

Procedural analysis

For goals that are performed as a sequence of steps, list the steps in order, with the decisions at each branch. Use a flowchart or a numbered list with sub-steps. For each step, note the inputs (what the learner needs to see or know), the action, and the result that signals the step is complete.

Example fragment, medication administration:

  1. Verify patient identity by scanning the wristband. - 1.1 If the scan succeeds and matches, proceed to step 2. - 1.2 If the scan fails to read, re-scan; after two failures, use the manual override procedure (step 1.3). - 1.3 Manual override: enter the medical record number, confirm two identifiers verbally, document the override reason.
  2. Scan the medication barcode. - 2.1 If a mismatch alert appears, stop; do not administer; follow the alert workflow.

Procedural analysis reveals branch points, which are where errors happen and where practice should concentrate. It also exposes steps that the expert performs automatically and would never think to teach.

Hierarchical analysis

For intellectual skills, start with the goal and ask repeatedly: "What must the learner already be able to do in order to learn this?" Each answer is a subordinate skill; place it below the goal and ask the question again. Stop when you reach the entry skills the learners already have (from your learner analysis). The result is a hierarchy in which lower skills must be learned before higher ones.

Example: to decide whether a mismatch alert requires stopping, the learner must be able to interpret the alert type, which requires distinguishing wrong-patient, wrong-drug, and wrong-time alerts, which requires reading the alert display, which is an entry skill.

Cluster analysis

For verbal information, group the items into meaningful clusters (by function, by location, by time) so that they can be taught and remembered as sets. Clusters often map onto job aids.

Cognitive task analysis

Experts make decisions they cannot easily articulate. Cognitive task analysis (CTA) uses structured interviews, think-aloud protocols, and critical-incident recall to surface the cues experts attend to, the decisions they make, and the errors novices make at the same points. CTA is expensive and is reserved for complex, high-stakes tasks, but even a light version (asking an expert to narrate a recent difficult case and probing at each decision) improves any analysis. Clark and colleagues summarize the evidence that instruction based on CTA outperforms instruction based on expert self-report.

Step 3: Identify entry skills

Draw a line across the bottom of your hierarchy. Everything below it is assumed; everything above it is taught. Where you draw the line comes from the learner analysis. If learners vary widely, you may need two lines and two paths.

Step 4: Check the analysis

  • Completeness. Could a novice perform the goal using only what is in the analysis? Have an expert and a novice review it.
  • Level of detail. Steps should be small enough to teach and assess, large enough to be meaningful. "Click OK" is too small; "administer medication" is too large.
  • Accuracy. Observe the task performed. Analyses built from documentation alone miss workarounds and tacit steps.
  • Decisions and errors. Every branch point should be explicit, and the common errors at each should be noted; they become practice items and assessment distractors.

Representing the analysis

Use whichever representation fits the outcome type:

  • Flowchart for procedures with branches.
  • Tree diagram for hierarchies.
  • Table with columns for step, cues, action, decision, common errors, and outcome type.
  • Outline for clusters of information.

Whatever the form, number every element so objectives can reference them in Module 4.

Common mistakes

  • Listing topics ("the medication module") instead of performances.
  • Stopping decomposition too early, so that the first objective is unteachable in one lesson.
  • Omitting decisions and error handling; procedures are taught as the happy path and fail in practice.
  • Analyzing from documentation without observing or interviewing performers.
  • Ignoring the attitudes component; many performance failures are choices, not skill gaps.

Preparing for Assignment 6

Choose one goal from your course design project. Classify it, decompose it with the appropriate method to at least three levels, mark the entry-skill line, and have at least one performer review the result.

References

Clark, R. E., Feldon, D. F., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., Yates, K. A., & Early, S. (2008). Cognitive task analysis. In J. M. Spector et al. (Eds.), Handbook of research on educational communications and technology (3rd ed., pp. 577–593). Routledge.

Dick, W., Carey, L., & Carey, J. O. (2015). The systematic design of instruction (8th ed.). Pearson. Chapters 3 and 4.

Gagne, R. M., Wager, W. W., Golas, K. C., & Keller, J. M. (2005). Principles of instructional design (5th ed.). Wadsworth.

Jonassen, D. H., Tessmer, M., & Hannum, W. H. (1999). Task analysis methods for instructional design. Lawrence Erlbaum.

Quiz

Module 3 Knowledge Check

Eight questions on learner, context, and task analysis. Unlimited attempts; best score counts.

1.

Interviews say learners are confident with a procedure; error logs show they fail it frequently. What should the designer do?

Answer: Trust the error logs and investigate why the confidence exists
Triangulate, and when self-report conflicts with performance data, believe the performance data and ask why.
2.

The performance context is:

Answer: The setting where learners will use what they learned
The performance context is where transfer must occur. If it does not support the new behavior, training will not produce it.
3.

Matching instruction to learners' self-reported learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) is well supported by research as a way to improve learning.

Answer: False
Reviews such as Pashler et al. (2008) found no credible evidence for the matching hypothesis. Preferences may inform engagement but not the design of instruction.
4.

According to Gagne's taxonomy, deciding whether a scanned wristband matches the medication order is primarily which type of outcome?

Answer: Intellectual skill
Making a rule-governed decision is an intellectual skill. Operating the scanner is the motor skill; choosing to scan every time is the attitude.
5.

Which question drives hierarchical analysis?

Answer: What must the learner already be able to do in order to learn this?
Asking that question repeatedly produces the hierarchy of subordinate skills down to the entry-skill line.
6.

Procedural analysis is most likely to reveal:

Answer: Branch points and decisions where errors occur
Branch points are where practice should concentrate and where assessment distractors come from.
7.

Which are appropriate ways to check a task analysis? Select all that apply.

Answer: Have an expert and a novice review it; Observe the task being performed; Ask whether a novice could perform the goal using only what is in the analysis
Completeness, accuracy through observation, and expert and novice review. Page length is not a validity check.
8.

Where does the entry-skill line in a hierarchy come from?

Answer: The learner analysis
Entry skills are what learners already have; that is a finding of the learner analysis.

Module 4: Objectives and Aligned Assessment

Write objectives that can be taught and measured, and design assessments that match them.

Page

Writing Learning Objectives

Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

What an objective is for

A learning objective states what the learner will be able to do after instruction, under what conditions, and to what standard. It is written for three audiences at once. It tells the designer what to teach and assess. It tells the learner what success looks like. And it tells the evaluator what to measure. An objective that cannot serve all three is not finished.

Objectives are derived directly from the task analysis: each numbered element above the entry-skill line becomes one or more objectives. That derivation is what keeps instruction tied to performance.

Two formats

Mager's three components

Robert Mager (1962) specified that a useful objective contains:

  1. Performance. What the learner will do, stated with an observable verb.
  2. Conditions. The circumstances under which the performance occurs: tools available, information given, constraints imposed.
  3. Criterion. How well the performance must be done: accuracy, speed, quality, or a standard to match.

Example: Given a patient wristband, a medication order in the EHR, and a handheld scanner (conditions), the nurse will verify patient identity and medication match (performance) with 100% accuracy across ten simulated administrations, including two with mismatch alerts (criterion).

The ABCD format

Heinich and colleagues' ABCD format adds the audience explicitly: Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree. It is the same information reorganized; many organizations prefer it because it forces the writer to name who the objective is for. Use whichever your context expects, but include all components.

Observable verbs

The verb is the objective. "Understand," "know," "appreciate," and "be familiar with" describe internal states nobody can observe. Replace them with what the learner would do to show the state: list, describe, classify, compare, calculate, demonstrate, perform, diagnose, design, justify.

Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) organizes cognitive verbs by complexity:

LevelWhat the learner doesSample verbs
RememberRetrieve factslist, name, recall, identify
UnderstandConstruct meaningdescribe, explain, summarize, classify, compare
ApplyUse a procedureperform, execute, calculate, demonstrate, use
AnalyzeBreak into parts and relate themdifferentiate, organize, diagnose, distinguish
EvaluateJudge against criteriacritique, justify, appraise, recommend
CreatePut elements together into something newdesign, compose, plan, produce

The taxonomy is a vocabulary, not a hierarchy to climb in every lesson. Match the level to the task analysis. If the job requires applying a procedure, an "apply" objective is correct; adding "create" objectives to look rigorous misaligns the instruction.

For Gagné's other domains use verbs suited to them: for motor skills, perform, execute, assemble; for attitudes, choose, volunteer, comply with; for verbal information, state, list, describe.

Writing objectives from the task analysis

  1. Take each element above the entry-skill line.
  2. Decide whether it deserves its own objective or folds into a parent. Rule of thumb: if it will be practiced and assessed separately, it gets an objective.
  3. Write the performance with a verb matched to the outcome type and level.
  4. Add the conditions that will actually be present at assessment and, ideally, on the job.
  5. Add a criterion that reflects the real standard. Not everything is 100%; not everything is "to the instructor's satisfaction."
  6. Number the objective with the task analysis element it came from (for example, Objective 2.1.3).

Terminal and enabling objectives

The terminal objective describes the goal performance; there is usually one per unit of instruction. Enabling objectives describe the subordinate skills that build to it. The hierarchy from your task analysis gives you the structure for free. Learners see the terminal objective and the main enabling objectives; the designer works with all of them.

Common flaws and fixes

Flawed objectiveFlawFixed objective
Students will understand the ADDIE modelUnobservable verb; no conditions or criterionGiven a description of an ID project, students will identify which ADDIE phase each described activity belongs to, with at least 9 of 10 correct
Learners will be familiar with the EHRUnobservable; topic rather than performanceUsing the practice environment, learners will locate a named patient and open the medication administration record within 60 seconds
Participants will learn about accessibilityVerb describes the instruction, not the learnerGiven a short e-learning module, participants will identify all WCAG violations from a list of eight common types
Nurses will administer medicationsMissing conditions and criterion; too broad(Split into the terminal objective and enabling objectives from the task analysis)
Students will write a good essay"Good" is not a criterionStudents will write a 500-word persuasive essay that meets all four criteria on the attached rubric at the proficient level or above

Objectives and motivation

Well-written objectives make relevance visible (Keller's R in ARCS) and give learners a standard to aim at, which supports confidence (C). Share the terminal objective and the assessment criteria with learners at the start of instruction. Hiding the standard helps nobody.

Preparing for the Objective Clinic

Write three objectives from your task analysis: the terminal objective and two enabling objectives. Post them in the clinic for peer critique before you use them in the instructional plan.

References

Anderson, L. W., & Krathwohl, D. R. (Eds.). (2001). A taxonomy for learning, teaching, and assessing: A revision of Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives. Longman.

Heinich, R., Molenda, M., Russell, J. D., & Smaldino, S. E. (2002). Instructional media and technologies for learning (7th ed.). Merrill.

Mager, R. F. (1997). Preparing instructional objectives (3rd ed.). Center for Effective Performance.

Page

Assessment Alignment and Rubrics

Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

Assessment comes before strategy

In Dick and Carey, assessment instruments are developed immediately after objectives and before instructional strategies. Backward Design makes the same move: decide what evidence you will accept before you plan activities. The reason is alignment. If the assessment is designed last, it tends to measure what was convenient to teach rather than what the objective required, and learners learn to the test rather than to the performance.

An assessment is aligned when the performance it elicits, the conditions it imposes, and the standard it applies match the objective. Check all three, every time.

Types of assessment by purpose

TypeWhenPurpose
Entry-skill testBefore instructionConfirm learners have the prerequisites; route those who do not
PretestBefore instructionMeasure what learners already know of the objectives; allow test-out; provide a baseline
Practice tests and embedded checksDuring instructionGive learners feedback and the designer formative data; retrieval practice improves retention
PosttestAfter instructionMeasure achievement of the objectives
Performance assessmentAfter instruction, or on the jobMeasure the actual performance under realistic conditions

Not every project needs all five. Every project needs the last two, and most benefit from embedded checks.

Criterion-referenced, not norm-referenced

Instructional design uses criterion-referenced assessment: each learner is measured against the standard in the objective, not against other learners. Grading on a curve makes no sense when the question is whether a nurse can administer medication safely. The criterion in the objective is the passing standard; if learners fail in large numbers, the instruction is the problem, not the learners.

Matching item types to objectives

Objective typeAppropriate assessmentInappropriate assessment
Verbal information (state, list, describe)Short answer, matching, multiple choice, completionExtended performance tasks
Intellectual skill: discrimination and concept classificationClassify new examples and non-examples; multiple choice with well-designed distractorsRecall of the definition alone
Intellectual skill: rule use and problem solvingSolve new problems; scenario-based items; worked cases with a decisionItems that repeat examples used in instruction
Motor skillObserved performance with a checklistWritten description of the procedure
AttitudeObserved choice in realistic situations; behavioral records over time; self-report as supplement onlyA quiz on what the right attitude is
Create-level cognitive objectivesProducts judged with a rubricMultiple choice

The most common alignment error is testing a rule-use objective with a recall item. If the objective says "decide," the assessment must present a decision.

Writing good selected-response items

  • Stem states a complete problem; the learner should be able to answer before reading the options.
  • Options are parallel in length and grammar; the correct answer is not the longest.
  • Distractors are plausible and, ideally, drawn from the common errors identified in the task analysis. A distractor no one chooses is wasted.
  • Avoid "all of the above," "none of the above," and negatives in the stem.
  • One item, one objective. Tag each item with the objective number so you can analyze results by objective.

Performance assessment and rubrics

When the objective is a performance or product, the assessment is a task plus a scoring guide.

Checklists list the required steps or features; each is present or absent. Use for procedures with a correct sequence.

Rating scales score each criterion on a scale (for example, 1 to 4) without describing the levels. Fast, but unreliable across raters.

Analytic rubrics describe each criterion at each level of performance. They are the most reliable and give the most useful feedback. Every assignment rubric in this course is analytic. Build one by:

  1. Listing the criteria from the objective and task analysis (three to six is typical).
  2. Describing the exemplary level for each criterion in observable terms.
  3. Describing the beginning level.
  4. Filling in the intermediate levels by naming what is present and what is missing.
  5. Testing the rubric on two or three real or simulated samples with a second rater, and revising where you disagree.

Holistic rubrics give one overall score with a description per level. Faster to apply, less diagnostic. Use for large-scale screening, not for feedback.

Feedback

Assessment during instruction is only formative if the learner gets feedback they can use. Effective feedback is specific to the criterion, tells the learner what to do next, and arrives while the learner can still act on it. Automated feedback in quizzes should explain why the correct answer is correct and why the chosen distractor is wrong; the knowledge checks in this course model that pattern.

Validity, reliability, and fairness

  • Validity: the assessment measures the objective. Alignment is the main validity check for instructional assessment.
  • Reliability: the assessment gives consistent results across items, occasions, and raters. Enough items per objective, clear rubrics, and rater training are the levers.
  • Fairness: the assessment does not disadvantage learners for reasons unrelated to the objective (reading load, cultural references, inaccessible formats). Apply the UDL principle of multiple means of action and expression where the objective allows.

Preparing for the instructional plan

For each objective in your plan (Module 6) you will specify an assessment: the type, the item or task, and the scoring guide. Draft one now for your terminal objective and bring it to the Objective Clinic along with the objectives.

References

Dick, W., Carey, L., & Carey, J. O. (2015). The systematic design of instruction (8th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 7.

Haladyna, T. M., & Rodriguez, M. C. (2013). Developing and validating test items. Routledge.

Shute, V. J. (2008). Focus on formative feedback. Review of Educational Research, 78(1), 153–189.

Wiggins, G., & McTighe, J. (2005). Understanding by design (2nd ed.). ASCD.

Quiz

Module 4 Knowledge Check

Eight questions on objectives and aligned assessment. Unlimited attempts; best score counts.

1.

Which objective contains all three of Mager's components?

Answer: Given an e-learning module, participants will identify all WCAG violations from a list of eight common types
Condition (given a module), performance (identify violations), criterion (all, from a list of eight).
2.

Which verbs describe observable performance? Select all that apply.

Answer: Classify; Demonstrate; Diagnose
Classify, demonstrate, and diagnose are observable. Understand, appreciate, and be familiar with describe internal states.
3.

A task analysis shows the job requires applying a procedure. The designer writes objectives at the 'create' level of Bloom's taxonomy to make the course more rigorous. This is:

Answer: Misalignment; the objective level should match the task analysis
The taxonomy is a vocabulary for matching, not a ladder to climb. Objectives derive from the task analysis.
4.

In the Dick and Carey model, assessment instruments are developed after the instructional strategy is chosen.

Answer: False
Assessments come right after objectives and before strategies, to guarantee alignment.
5.

An objective asks learners to decide whether a mismatch alert requires stopping. Which assessment is aligned?

Answer: Given six new scenarios with alerts, decide in each whether to stop, with a rationale
A decision objective needs an assessment that presents decisions, with new scenarios rather than the ones used in instruction.
6.

Criterion-referenced assessment means:

Answer: Each learner is measured against the standard stated in the objective
The criterion in the objective is the standard. If many learners fail, examine the instruction.
7.

Where should the distractors for a multiple-choice item ideally come from?

Answer: Common errors identified in the task analysis
Distractors built from real errors are diagnostic. A distractor nobody chooses is wasted.
8.

Which scoring guide describes each criterion at each level of performance?

Answer: Analytic rubric
Analytic rubrics are the most reliable and give the most useful feedback.
Discussion forum

Objective Clinic

The Objective Clinic is a peer workshop. Everyone brings objectives; everyone leaves with better ones.

Initial post (by midweek). Post three objectives from your task analysis: the terminal objective and two enabling objectives. Number each with its task analysis element. For the terminal objective, also post a draft assessment: the type, a description of the task or a sample item, and the scoring approach.

Replies (by end of module). Critique two classmates' sets. For each objective, check:

  1. Is the verb observable and matched to the outcome type and level?
  2. Are the conditions stated, and do they reflect what will be present at assessment and on the job?
  3. Is the criterion a real standard, not "correctly" or "to the instructor's satisfaction"?
  4. Is the draft assessment aligned on performance, conditions, and standard?

Rewrite at least one of their objectives as you would phrase it, and explain the change. Be direct and specific; this is a workshop, and vague praise helps nobody.

Revision. Edit your original post to add a "Revised" section with your improved objectives before the module closes. Graded on the quality of your critiques and the improvement in your revision (part of the discussions and knowledge checks component).

Module 5: ID Case Analysis II

A second, more complex case that adds organizational politics, technology, and evaluation pressure.

Page

Case 2: Scaling AI Literacy at Pinewood Community College

This case is fictional. Any resemblance to real organizations or people is coincidental.

The request

Pinewood Community College enrolls about 9,400 students across a main campus, two satellite centers, and a large online program. It employs 118 full-time faculty and roughly 310 adjuncts. In August, the Vice President for Academic Affairs, Dr. Renee Castillo, announced an "AI Literacy Initiative" with three goals: every course syllabus would include an AI-use policy by January; every faculty member would complete "AI literacy professional development" by May; and the college would report to its accreditor, in the spring, on how it was "preparing students for an AI-influenced workforce."

Jordan Lee, the college's instructional designer in the Center for Teaching and Learning (CTL), was asked to design the professional development. The CTL has three staff: Jordan, a director named Priya Natarajan who also teaches two sections of English each term, and a part-time technologist who supports the LMS. The initiative has a $40,000 budget for the year, most of which Dr. Castillo expects to spend on "a platform or a partner."

What Jordan learned

Faculty survey (September, 241 responses of 428, 56%). Asked to describe their stance on generative AI in their courses:

StanceFull-timeAdjunct
Ban it; it is cheating31%38%
Allow with restrictions44%35%
Encourage and teach it18%12%
Have not thought about it7%15%

Asked what they wanted from professional development, the top responses were "how to detect AI cheating" (63%), "how to write an AI policy" (58%), "examples from my discipline" (51%), and "how to use AI to save time on grading and prep" (47%). Only 22% selected "how to teach students to use AI well." Free-text responses included "I am not going to learn a tool that will be replaced next year," "I have 180 students and no time," and "Just tell me what the college policy is and I'll put it in the syllabus."

Focus groups (three, 24 faculty). Themes: fear of being blamed for student misconduct; resentment of past mandatory training ("the last one was a 45-minute video with a quiz that anyone could pass by guessing"); real curiosity among a minority who had experimented; frustration among nursing, welding, and automotive faculty that the initiative seemed aimed at "writing classes"; and strong doubt that AI detection tools work. Two adjuncts said they teach at three colleges and could not attend anything synchronous.

Students. A student government survey (n = 612) found 71% used generative AI for coursework at least monthly; 48% said they were unsure whether their use was allowed; 29% had received contradictory instructions from different instructors in the same term.

Existing resources. The library had run four well-attended "AI 101" webinars. Three faculty (in English, business, and computer information systems) had already redesigned assignments around AI and were willing to share. The CTL's LMS could host self-paced modules with completion tracking. A vendor had pitched a "turnkey AI literacy course for faculty" (12 hours of video modules, generic across disciplines, $28,000 per year, completion certificates included). Dr. Castillo liked that it "solves the reporting problem."

Accreditation. The accreditor's request was open-ended: describe what the college is doing to prepare students for the workforce, including with respect to emerging technologies. There was no requirement that every faculty member complete anything.

Governance. The Faculty Senate had formed an AI committee that met twice and produced no recommendations. Its chair told Jordan, "If Academic Affairs mandates a training, we will fight it. If you ask us to help design it, we will."

The complication

In October, a well-publicized incident occurred: an adjunct instructor accused nine students of AI-generated work based on a detection tool's score; three of the accusations were later withdrawn after the students produced drafts and version histories. The college newspaper ran the story. Dr. Castillo emailed Jordan: "This is exactly why we need everyone trained, and soon. Can we move the faculty completion deadline to March? I would like to see a plan by the end of next week. The vendor option is still on the table and honestly it would be simplest."

Jordan has $40,000, a part-time technologist, a director with a full teaching load, a divided faculty, three willing champions, a hostile-but-persuadable Senate, a vendor, and eight days to produce a plan.

Questions to consider

Use the six-step framework. Additional prompts specific to this case:

  • What is the performance gap? Whose performance? Is it primarily a knowledge and skill gap, or something else?
  • The faculty asked for detection and policy; the initiative's stated goal is student preparation. How do you reconcile what learners want with what the organization needs, and with what the evidence supports?
  • What are the risks of the vendor course, beyond cost? What are its genuine advantages?
  • How would you handle the difference between full-time and adjunct faculty, and among disciplines?
  • What role could the three champions, the library, and the Senate committee play, and what would it cost to involve them?
  • What evidence would satisfy the accreditor, and does it require universal completion?
  • How does the October incident change the priorities, if at all?
  • What would you tell Dr. Castillo about the March deadline?
Discussion forum

Case 2 Discussion: Stakeholders and Trade-offs

The Pinewood case has more stakeholders with more conflicting interests than Crestview. Map them before you analyze.

Initial post (by midweek). Post a stakeholder table with at least seven rows: stakeholder, what they want, what they fear, and what they could contribute. Then answer in no more than 200 words: which two stakeholders' interests are most in conflict, and what design choice would you make to manage that conflict?

Replies (by end of module). Reply to two classmates. Identify one stakeholder or interest they missed or characterized differently from you, and say whether the difference would change the recommendation. Comment on whether their conflict-management choice is realistic given the budget and the eight-day deadline.

Assignment - 100 points

Assignment 4: ID Case Analysis II

Write a case analysis of "Scaling AI Literacy at Pinewood Community College" using the six-step framework. Your analysis should read as the plan Jordan will send Dr. Castillo at the end of the week, with an executive summary she can read in two minutes.

Requirements

  • 1,800 to 2,400 words, with an executive summary of no more than 200 words at the top and a heading for each of the six steps.
  • Cite evidence from the case at every step, including the survey data.
  • Apply at least three concepts from Modules 1 through 4 by name. Learner analysis and the distinction between what learners request and what the performance requires must appear.
  • In step 4, propose at least three alternatives; one must include the vendor option and one must address the adjunct and disciplinary differences explicitly. For each, estimate cost against the $40,000 budget.
  • In step 5, include a response to the March deadline and a plan for involving at least one of: the champions, the library, the Senate committee.
  • In step 6, describe what evidence you would present to the accreditor and how you would know by May whether the initiative worked.
  • APA 7 for outside sources. AI-use disclosure if applicable. Given the topic, you are encouraged to use an AI tool for some part of your process and to reflect briefly on what it contributed and where it was wrong.

Submission

PDF or Google Doc link.

Rubric (100 points)
