Module 6: Creating Instruction: Planning and Designing the Intervention

Instructional strategies, multimedia and accessibility principles, and rapid prototyping.

Page

Instructional Strategies: Gagne, Merrill, and Scaffolding

Estimated reading time: 35 minutes.

What an instructional strategy is

An instructional strategy is the plan for how learners will get from their entry skills to the objectives: the sequence of content, the events that happen in each lesson, the kinds of practice and feedback, the grouping, and the media. Dick and Carey place it after assessment so that every strategy decision can be checked against "does this help learners perform on the assessment, and therefore on the job?"

Three frameworks organize most strategy decisions: Gagné's nine events for the structure of a lesson, Merrill's First Principles for the quality of the whole, and the cognitive research on practice, feedback, and scaffolding for the details.

Gagné's nine events of instruction

Gagné argued that learning requires a sequence of internal processes (attention, expectancy, retrieval, encoding, responding, reinforcement, retrieval cues, generalization) and that instruction should supply external events that support each. The nine events:

EventPurposeExamples
1. Gain attentionOrient the learnerA surprising fact, a problem, a short scenario, a question
2. Inform learners of the objectiveSet expectancyState what they will be able to do and why it matters
3. Stimulate recall of prior learningActivate relevant knowledgeQuick review, a question about experience, a pretest item
4. Present the contentProvide the stimulusExplanation, demonstration, worked example, reading, video
5. Provide learning guidanceSupport encodingAnalogies, cues, examples and non-examples, concept maps, hints
6. Elicit performanceHave learners respondPractice problems, simulations, role-play, application tasks
7. Provide feedbackReinforce and correctSpecific, timely feedback on the practice
8. Assess performanceConfirm learningPosttest, performance assessment
9. Enhance retention and transferSupport generalizationVaried practice, spaced review, application to new contexts, job aids

The events are not a rigid script. A lesson may cycle through events 4 through 7 several times, and a problem-based lesson may start at event 6. But a lesson missing events 6 and 7 (practice and feedback) is a presentation, not instruction, and lessons missing event 9 rarely transfer.

Merrill's First Principles as a strategy check

Apply the five principles to the whole unit, not just each lesson:

  • Problem-centered. Is the instruction organized around a progression of real tasks, from simple to complex, rather than around topics? Show the whole task early, even if learners cannot yet do it.
  • Activation. Do learners recall or share relevant experience before new content? Do you surface misconceptions?
  • Demonstration. Do learners see the skill performed, with the expert's reasoning made visible, and with examples matched to the outcome type (worked examples for procedures, examples and non-examples for concepts)?
  • Application. Do learners perform the task with coaching that fades? Is practice varied across contexts?
  • Integration. Do learners reflect on, discuss, defend, or adapt what they learned? Do they carry something back into their own world?

Evidence-based practice design

The cognitive research on learning is consistent on several points that strategy should honor:

  • Retrieval practice. Recalling information strengthens retention far more than rereading it. Build low-stakes retrieval into every lesson.
  • Spacing. Practice distributed over time beats the same practice massed. Return to earlier objectives in later lessons.
  • Interleaving. Mixing problem types during practice improves discrimination and transfer, even though it feels harder.
  • Worked examples and fading. Novices learn procedures faster from studying worked examples than from unguided problem solving; as expertise grows, fade the examples into completion problems and then full problems.
  • Feedback. Specific, timely, and focused on the task and the process; not on the person. Delayed feedback can be as effective as immediate for retention if the learner engages with it.
  • Cognitive load. Working memory is limited. Remove extraneous load (decorative graphics, split attention between text and diagram, redundant narration of on-screen text), manage intrinsic load (sequence from simple to complex, pre-teach component skills), and use the freed capacity for germane processing (self-explanation, comparison).

Scaffolding and cognitive apprenticeship

Scaffolding is support that lets learners perform beyond their current unaided ability and that is withdrawn as competence grows. Cognitive apprenticeship (Collins, Brown, and Newman) names the moves: modeling (the expert performs and thinks aloud), coaching (guided practice with feedback), scaffolding and fading, articulation (learners explain their reasoning), reflection (learners compare their process with the expert's), and exploration (learners frame and solve their own problems). This sequence is a strong default for complex skills and is compatible with Gagné's events.

Sequencing content

  • Procedural tasks: sequence in the order performed, with branch decisions taught where they occur.
  • Hierarchical skills: teach subordinate skills before the skills that depend on them, but show the whole task first so learners know why.
  • Concepts: teach the defining attributes, then examples and non-examples with increasing subtlety, then classification practice.
  • Whole-task approaches (van Merriënboer's Four-Component Instructional Design): sequence a series of complete tasks from simple to complex, with supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice provided just in time. Preferred for complex skills where component practice alone does not transfer.

Grouping and delivery

Strategy includes who learns with whom and where: self-paced, instructor-led, cohort-based, blended. Decide based on the learner and context analysis. Collaboration helps when the task benefits from multiple perspectives or when articulation is a goal; it hurts when it adds coordination load to a task that does not need it. Online delivery requires deliberate design for social presence and for the self-regulation that self-paced learning demands.

Media selection

Choose media after strategy, not before. The question is not "should we use video?" but "what does event 4 (presentation) or event 6 (practice) require, and which medium supports it best at acceptable cost?" Clark's long-standing argument is that media do not cause learning; methods do. Media constrain which methods are feasible. A simulation is worth building when the practice it enables cannot be provided otherwise; a video is worth producing when demonstration of a dynamic process is needed and text cannot convey it.

Writing the strategy for your plan

For each lesson or unit in your instructional plan, specify:

  1. The objectives covered.
  2. The nine events (which are present, how each is done, how long).
  3. The practice and feedback design (type, quantity, spacing, fading).
  4. The grouping and delivery mode.
  5. The media, with a one-sentence justification tied to the event it serves.

Then check the whole plan against Merrill's principles and against cognitive load.

References

Clark, R. E. (1994). Media will never influence learning. Educational Technology Research and Development, 42(2), 21–29.

Collins, A., Brown, J. S., & Newman, S. E. (1989). Cognitive apprenticeship. In L. B. Resnick (Ed.), Knowing, learning, and instruction (pp. 453–494). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

Gagne, R. M., Wager, W. W., Golas, K. C., & Keller, J. M. (2005). Principles of instructional design (5th ed.). Wadsworth.

Merrill, M. D. (2002). First principles of instruction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 50(3), 43–59.

Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292.

van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Kirschner, P. A. (2018). Ten steps to complex learning (3rd ed.). Routledge.

Page

Designing E-Learning: Multimedia, UDL, and Accessibility

Estimated reading time: 30 minutes. Browse the UDL Guidelines and the WCAG at-a-glance page (linked in this module) alongside this page.

Multimedia learning: Mayer's principles

Richard Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning rests on three assumptions: people process words and pictures in separate channels; each channel has limited capacity; and learning requires active processing (selecting, organizing, integrating). From decades of experiments Mayer derived principles for designing instruction that combines words and pictures. The most useful for practice:

PrincipleGuidanceDesign implication
MultimediaPeople learn better from words and pictures than from words aloneAdd a relevant diagram, not a decorative photo
CoherenceExclude extraneous words, pictures, and soundsCut background music, tangential anecdotes, decorative clip art
SignalingHighlight the organization of essential materialHeadings, arrows, bold key terms, an outline that persists
RedundancyDo not present the same words as on-screen text and narrationNarrate a diagram; do not narrate a slide of text
Spatial contiguityPlace words near the pictures they describeLabels on the diagram, not in a legend across the page
Temporal contiguityPresent corresponding words and pictures at the same timeNarration synchronized with animation, not before or after
SegmentingPresent in learner-paced segments rather than a continuous unitShort chunks with a "continue" control
Pre-trainingTeach the names and characteristics of key components firstA short glossary or component tour before the process animation
ModalityPresent words as narration rather than on-screen text when paired with graphicsNarrated animation beats captioned animation for novices (with a caption option for accessibility)
PersonalizationUse conversational rather than formal style"You will see..." rather than "The learner will observe..."
VoiceUse a human voice rather than a machine voiceApplies to narration; test synthetic voices before using them

These principles reduce extraneous cognitive load and direct attention. They apply to slides, videos, e-learning modules, job aids, and web pages. They apply with more force for novices; experts can tolerate, and sometimes prefer, denser presentations.

Universal Design for Learning

UDL (CAST) is a framework for designing instruction that works for the widest range of learners from the start, instead of retrofitting accommodations. Its three principles map onto the affective, recognition, and strategic networks of the brain:

  1. Multiple means of engagement (the "why"): options for recruiting interest, sustaining effort, and self-regulation. Examples: choice of topic within a task, relevance made explicit, clear goals and progress feedback.
  2. Multiple means of representation (the "what"): options for perception, language, and comprehension. Examples: captions and transcripts, text alternatives for images, glossaries, multiple examples, background knowledge supports.
  3. Multiple means of action and expression (the "how"): options for physical action, expression, and executive function. Examples: alternatives to mouse-only interaction, choice of product format where the objective allows, planning templates, checklists.

UDL is not "make three versions of everything." It is a set of checkpoints to consult during design so that the most common barriers are removed before anyone hits them. In your instructional plan you will pick two or three checkpoints and show how the design addresses them.

Accessibility: WCAG

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) define what makes digital content usable by people with disabilities. Version 2.2 is current; conformance at level AA is the standard in most institutional policies and in United States law for public entities. The four principles:

  • Perceivable. Text alternatives for images; captions and transcripts for audio and video; content that can be presented in different ways without losing meaning; sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 for normal text); no information conveyed by color alone.
  • Operable. Everything works with a keyboard; users have enough time; nothing flashes in ways that cause seizures; navigation is consistent and headings are meaningful.
  • Understandable. Language is identified; behavior is predictable; input errors are identified and explained.
  • Robust. Content works with current and future assistive technologies; use real headings, lists, and form labels rather than visual imitations.

Practical checklist for every e-learning asset:

  1. Every meaningful image has alt text; decorative images are marked decorative.
  2. Every video has accurate captions; every audio file has a transcript.
  3. Headings are real headings in a logical order.
  4. Color contrast passes; links are distinguishable without color.
  5. All interactions work with keyboard alone; focus is visible.
  6. Documents (PDF, Word, PowerPoint) are tagged and pass the built-in accessibility checker.
  7. Any drag-and-drop, timed, or motion-based interaction has an alternative.

Accessibility and Mayer's principles reinforce each other more often than they conflict. Where they seem to (modality says narrate, accessibility says caption), provide both: narration with captions the learner can toggle.

Tools for e-learning development

CategoryExamplesUse
Authoring toolsArticulate Storyline 360, Articulate Rise, Adobe Captivate, iSpringInteractive modules exported as SCORM or xAPI for an LMS
Open interactive contentH5PInteractive video, branching scenarios, quizzes; free and embeds in most LMSs
VideoCamtasia, OBS Studio, Loom, PanoptoScreencasts and lectures; add captions
Graphics and layoutCanva, Figma, PowerPointDiagrams, job aids, storyboards
Simulation and branchingStoryline, Twine, H5P Branching ScenarioDecision practice with consequences
Generative AIText, image, and voice modelsDrafting scripts, alt text, scenario variants, and synthetic narration; verify everything and disclose use

Tool choice follows strategy and media decisions. Storyline is powerful and expensive; Rise is fast and constrained; H5P is free and good enough for most interactions. Match the tool to the interaction the strategy requires, the skills of your team, and the budget.

Standards for packaging

Modules built in authoring tools are delivered to an LMS as SCORM packages (older, widely supported, tracks completion and score) or xAPI statements (newer, tracks richer activity, needs a learning record store). Course-level content is exchanged among LMSs as IMS Common Cartridge. Knowing these names lets you talk to LMS administrators and vendors.

Storyboarding and Rapid Prototyping

Estimated reading time: 20 minutes.

Why prototype

A design document describes instruction; a prototype lets people experience it. Stakeholders who approve a document often reject the module built from it, because the document did not make them imagine what learners would actually do. Prototypes surface those reactions early, when changes are cheap. They also expose problems the designer cannot see from the inside: an interaction that is confusing, a scenario that feels fake, a page that takes three times longer than planned.

Prototyping is the core of SAM and of rapid prototyping models; it also fits inside ADDIE and Dick and Carey as the front half of formative evaluation (Module 7). Whichever model you chose, plan to prototype.

Fidelity: how finished should it be?

FidelityFormWhat it testsCost
PaperSketches of screens, index cards for branches, a script read aloudSequence, flow, scenario plausibility, lengthMinutes to hours
LowSlides with placeholder graphics and clickable navigation; a text-only version of a branching scenarioInteraction logic, wording, decision pointsHours
MediumAuthoring-tool build with real text, draft graphics, temporary narration (or synthetic voice)Look and feel, timing, usabilityDays
HighNear-final module with produced mediaFinal polish, technical function, accessibilityWeeks

Start at the lowest fidelity that can answer your current question. Test the flow on paper before you write a single line in an authoring tool. Move up only when the lower-fidelity version stops producing useful findings.

Storyboards

A storyboard describes each screen or segment of instruction: what the learner sees, hears, and does, and what happens next. It is the handoff document between designer and developer and the primary artifact for stakeholder review. A useful storyboard row or page contains:

FieldContent
Screen IDUnique number tied to the lesson and objective (for example, L2-S07, Objective 2.1.3)
Gagne eventWhich of the nine events this screen serves
VisualDescription or sketch of what is on screen; image and graphic requirements
On-screen textExact text
Audio / narrationScript; note whether narration replaces or supplements text (Mayer's redundancy principle)
InteractionWhat the learner does: click, choose, type, drag; branching rules
FeedbackWhat appears for each response
NavigationWhere the learner goes next; whether they can go back
Accessibility notesAlt text, caption source, keyboard alternative for any interaction
Development notesAsset file names, tool-specific instructions

A storyboard for a 20-minute module runs 15 to 40 rows. Write it in a table (Word, Google Docs, or a spreadsheet) or in the authoring tool's own storyboard view.

Branching scenarios

Decision practice is where most e-learning fails to go beyond click-next. A branching scenario presents a situation, asks the learner to decide, shows the consequence, and continues. Design it from the task analysis: every branch point in your procedural analysis is a decision screen, and the common errors you recorded are the wrong options. Keep the structure manageable: three or four decisions with two or three options each and a few converging paths is plenty. Prototype it in Twine or on index cards before building.

Testing a prototype

Even a paper prototype should be tested with someone who resembles the learners. A one-to-one test takes 30 to 45 minutes:

  1. Explain that you are testing the design, not the person.
  2. Ask them to work through the prototype, thinking aloud.
  3. Do not help unless they are stuck for more than a minute; note where and why.
  4. Afterward, ask: what was confusing, what was too easy or too hard, what would they change, and can they perform the objective now?
  5. Record findings and decide what to change before the next iteration.

Three one-to-one tests find most of the serious problems. Module 7 expands this into a full formative evaluation plan.

Working with subject-matter experts

Most designers build content with a subject-matter expert (SME) rather than from their own knowledge. Practical rules: give the SME a specific task with a deadline (review this storyboard for accuracy; provide three realistic error cases), not an open request; explain design decisions in terms of learner performance so the SME understands why the module is not a lecture; separate accuracy review (the SME's call) from design review (yours); and prototype early so the SME reacts to something concrete.

Preparing for Assignment 7, Part 1

Your instructional plan includes a storyboard for one complete lesson and a low-fidelity prototype of at least one interaction. Choose the lesson that best represents your strategy, and choose the interaction that carries the most decision practice.

Module 6 Knowledge Check

Ten questions on strategies, multimedia, accessibility, and prototyping. Unlimited attempts; best score counts.

1.

A lesson presents content clearly and ends with a summary, but learners never practice or receive feedback. In Gagne's terms this lesson is missing:

Answer: Events 6 and 7
Eliciting performance (6) and providing feedback (7) are what make it instruction rather than presentation.
2.

Which practices are supported by the cognitive research summarized in this module? Select all that apply.

Answer: Retrieval practice; Spacing practice over time; Interleaving problem types; Studying worked examples before solving problems as a novice
Retrieval, spacing, interleaving, and worked examples with fading are well supported. Rereading is weak.
3.

Clark's argument that 'media will never influence learning' implies that designers should:

Answer: Choose media after deciding the method, based on what the method requires
Methods cause learning; media constrain which methods are feasible. Choose media to serve the events and practice the strategy requires.
4.

A narrated video shows a diagram while the same sentences appear as on-screen text. Which of Mayer's principles does this violate?

Answer: Redundancy
Presenting identical words as narration and on-screen text overloads the verbal channel. Narrate the diagram; keep captions as an accessibility option.
5.

Which is an example of the UDL principle of multiple means of action and expression?

Answer: Offering a choice of product format where the objective allows
Choice of how to demonstrate learning is action and expression. Captions and glossaries are representation; relevance is engagement.
6.

Which items belong on the accessibility checklist for an e-learning asset? Select all that apply.

Answer: Alt text for meaningful images; Accurate captions for video; Keyboard operation for all interactions; Real headings in logical order
Alt text, captions, keyboard operability, and real headings. Background music violates Mayer's coherence principle and can interfere with screen readers.
7.

The minimum WCAG color contrast ratio for normal text at level AA is 4.5:1.

Answer: True
Correct. Large text may use 3:1.
8.

You want to test whether the sequence and decision points of a branching scenario make sense before spending days in an authoring tool. What fidelity of prototype should you use?

Answer: Paper or low fidelity (index cards, text-only, or clickable slides)
Start at the lowest fidelity that answers the question. Sequence and logic can be tested on paper.
9.

Where should the wrong options in a branching scenario's decision screens come from?

Answer: The common errors recorded at branch points in the task analysis
Real errors make realistic, diagnostic distractors and connect the practice to the performance.
10.

Which standard packages an authoring-tool module so an LMS can track completion and score?

Answer: SCORM
SCORM (or xAPI with a learning record store). Common Cartridge exchanges whole courses between LMSs.

4. Multimedia and accessibility

  • A short note on what you learned from building the prototype.

6. Implementation notes

  • What facilitators, learners, and administrators need in order to run the instruction (a facilitator guide outline, learner instructions, technical requirements).
  • Project timeline and resources for full development, in a simple table.

Format

Module 7: Evaluation: Determining the Effect of the Intervention

Formative and summative evaluation, peer review, and the final reflection on your plan.

Page

Formative and Summative Evaluation

Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

Two questions, two evaluations

Formative evaluation asks: how can this instruction be improved before it is finished? It happens during design and development and its audience is the design team.

Summative evaluation asks: did the finished instruction work, and is it worth continuing? It happens after implementation and its audience is the decision makers who fund and mandate the instruction.

Both are part of the design, not afterthoughts. Dick and Carey give each its own component and make revision a loop that formative evaluation feeds. Every plan you write in practice should say when and how both will happen.

Formative evaluation: three stages

Dick and Carey's three-stage sequence is the standard.

One-to-one evaluation

Work through the draft instruction with one learner at a time, three or so learners representing the range of the target population (one above average, one average, one below on entry skills). Sit beside them, ask them to think aloud, and note errors, confusions, pacing problems, and their reactions. Ask about clarity, impact, and feasibility. Give the posttest. This stage catches the gross errors: wrong content, unclear instructions, missing steps, examples that do not work.

Small-group evaluation

After revising, try the instruction with 8 to 20 learners under conditions close to real use, with the designer observing but not intervening. Collect the pretest and posttest, item-level results, time on task, and a short attitude survey. This stage tests whether the revisions worked and whether the instruction functions without the designer present. Analyze results by objective: which objectives were achieved, which were not, and what in the instruction accounts for it.

Field trial

Try the revised instruction with a full group (30 or more) in the actual setting, delivered by the intended facilitators or the intended self-paced system. The designer is absent or a distant observer. This stage tests implementation: facilitator guides, logistics, technology, and the effect of the real context. Collect the same data as the small group plus facilitator feedback.

Expert review

Alongside learner-based stages, have a subject-matter expert check accuracy, a second instructional designer check alignment and strategy, and an accessibility reviewer check conformance. Expert review is fast and finds things learners cannot name.

Analyzing and using formative data

  • Build an item-by-objective table. An objective with low posttest success and adequate instruction time points to a strategy problem; low success with little time points to a coverage problem.
  • Compare pretest and posttest by objective, not only overall. A high overall gain can hide one objective nobody learned.
  • Pair every problem with a location in the instruction and a proposed revision. Revise, then retest the revised parts if the stakes justify it.
  • Keep a revision log; it is evidence for the summative report and for your own learning.

Summative evaluation

Summative evaluation judges the instruction against its purpose. The classic framework is Kirkpatrick's four levels, updated as the New World Kirkpatrick Model:

LevelQuestionTypical measures
1. ReactionDid learners find it engaging, relevant, and satisfactory?Post-instruction survey with specific items, not just "was it good"
2. LearningDid they acquire the intended knowledge, skills, attitudes, and confidence?Posttest, performance assessment, pre-post comparison
3. BehaviorDo they apply it on the job or in the next course?Observation, supervisor reports, work samples, system data, follow-up at 30 to 90 days
4. ResultsDid the targeted outcomes change?Error rates, help desk calls, performance metrics, retention, cost, the accreditor's criteria

Two cautions. First, level 1 alone tells you almost nothing about effectiveness; satisfaction and learning are only weakly related. Second, level 4 outcomes are affected by many factors besides instruction, so claim contribution, not sole cause, and design the evaluation so plausible alternative explanations can be addressed (a comparison group, a baseline, time-series data).

Summative evaluation has two phases in Dick and Carey's framing: an expert judgment phase (is the instruction congruent with the organization's needs, complete, accurate, and well designed?) and a field trial phase (does it produce the outcomes with the intended learners in the intended setting?).

Evaluation and the models

  • ADDIE: Evaluation is the fifth phase and also runs across the others.
  • Dick and Carey: components 8 (formative), 9 (revise), and 10 (summative).
  • SAM: evaluation is built into every iteration; the "evaluate" step in each cycle is formative, and the final implementation is evaluated summatively.
  • Backward Design: stage 2 (acceptable evidence) is the assessment design; program-level evaluation is added on top.

Designing an evaluation plan

For your project, the plan should specify:

  1. Formative: which stages you will run (at minimum one-to-one and small group, or a justified adaptation), with participants, instruments, data, and the decision rules for revision.
  2. Summative: the levels you will measure, the instruments, the timing, the comparison or baseline, and who receives the report.
  3. Logistics: who does what, when, at what cost, and what happens to the data (consent, storage, privacy).
  4. Reporting: the form of the report and the decisions it will inform.

An evaluation plan that can actually be carried out with the resources available beats an ambitious one that will not happen.

References

Dick, W., Carey, L., & Carey, J. O. (2015). The systematic design of instruction (8th ed.). Pearson. Chapters 10 to 12.

Kirkpatrick, J. D., & Kirkpatrick, W. K. (2016). Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation. ATD Press.

Tessmer, M. (1993). Planning and conducting formative evaluations. Kogan Page.

Peer Review Exchange

Peer review is an expert-review stage of formative evaluation, and it is also practice in giving the kind of feedback designers receive from colleagues.

Post (first three days of the module). Attach or link your Assignment 7, Part 1 instructional plan and prototype. Title the thread with your project title. Add three sentences telling reviewers where you most want feedback.

Review (by day seven). You will be assigned two peers' plans (see the pairing announcement). For each, complete the peer review form:

  1. Alignment. Check three objectives against their assessments and lessons. Report any mismatch specifically.
  2. Strategy. Pick one lesson. Which of Gagne's nine events are strong, which are weak or missing, and what would you add?
  3. Multimedia and accessibility. Name one Mayer principle the storyboard applies well and one it violates. Check the accessibility notes on three screens.
  4. Prototype. Work through the prototype as a learner. Where did you hesitate or get confused? Could you perform the objective afterward?
  5. Two strengths, two priority revisions. Be specific enough that the author can act without asking you what you meant.

Post the completed form as a reply in the author's thread. Reviews are graded as part of Assignment 7, Part 2. Authors respond to each review with one sentence acknowledging it and one sentence saying what they will change or why not.

Module 7 Knowledge Check

Eight questions on formative and summative evaluation. Unlimited attempts; best score counts.

1.

The primary audience for formative evaluation findings is:

Answer: The design team, to improve the instruction
Formative evaluation exists to improve instruction before it is finished.
2.

In Dick and Carey's sequence, which formative stage is designed to catch gross errors such as wrong content, unclear instructions, and examples that do not work?

Answer: One-to-one
One-to-one evaluation with three learners representing the range of the population finds the gross errors first.
3.

A small-group evaluation shows a large overall pre-post gain. What should the designer check before concluding the instruction works?

Answer: Results by objective, since an overall gain can hide an objective nobody learned
Analyze item-by-objective. Overall averages hide specific failures.
4.

Which are among Kirkpatrick's four levels? Select all that apply.

Answer: Reaction; Learning; Behavior; Results
Reaction, learning, behavior, and results. Cost is analyzed in return-on-investment extensions, not as a Kirkpatrick level.
5.

High learner satisfaction (level 1) is a reliable indicator that learning (level 2) occurred.

Answer: False
Satisfaction and learning are only weakly related. Measure learning directly.
6.

A help desk saw fewer calls after training was delivered, but a new job aid was released the same week. In a summative evaluation this is an example of:

Answer: An alternative explanation that the evaluation design must address
Level 4 outcomes are affected by many factors. Claim contribution, and design for comparisons or baselines that address alternatives.
7.

Which formative activity is fastest and finds problems learners cannot name, such as inaccurate content or misaligned assessments?

Answer: Expert review
Subject-matter, design, and accessibility expert reviews run alongside learner-based stages.
8.

What distinguishes a field trial from a small-group evaluation?

Answer: Field trials occur in the actual setting with the intended facilitators or system and the designer absent, testing implementation
The field trial tests whether the instruction works under real conditions without the designer present.

Course Completion and Next Steps

You have analyzed two design cases, studied real learners, decomposed a task, written aligned objectives and assessments, planned and prototyped instruction, and designed its evaluation. That is the full arc of instructional design practice.

Build your portfolio

Your instructional plan, storyboard, prototype, and evaluation plan are portfolio pieces. Before you file them away:

  • Remove any identifying information about the learners you studied.
  • Write a one-page project summary: the problem, your process, the design, and what the evaluation would show. Hiring managers read the summary, not the 30 pages.
  • Export the prototype in a form that will still open in two years (PDF of the storyboard, a video walkthrough of the interaction).

Where to go next

  • Advanced coursework. Courses in e-learning development (authoring tools, SCORM and xAPI), evaluation and assessment, learning analytics, and design-based research build directly on this one.
  • Professional community. The Association for Educational Communications and Technology (AECT) and the Association for Talent Development (ATD) publish standards, journals, and conference programs. AECT's Educational Technology Research and Development is the field's primary journal.
  • Standards. Review the IBSTPI instructional designer competencies and rate yourself; the gaps are your next learning objectives.
  • Practice. The fastest way to get better at instructional design is to design instruction, evaluate it, and revise it. Volunteer for a project in your organization within the next three months.

Thank you for your work this term. Keep the learners at the center, keep the analysis honest, and keep the loop closed.
